summary: This informational document discusses high-level problems and goals for active-active connection at the TRILL edge, extending multipath and fast failover to end stations that connect to a TRILL campus in more than one place.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains why a device connected to several TRILL edge switches can cause duplicate traffic and other problems. It lists the goals a future solution should meet.

questions: what is active-active connection in trill
what is the trill appointed forwarder problem
subtitle: The TRILL edge problems and goals for using multiple end-station links at once.

tldr.problem: A customer device connected through a local active-active link protocol can make multiple TRILL edge switches believe they are the Appointed Forwarder.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes four resulting problems and sets data-plane, control-plane, and deployment goals for future solutions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7379 is an Informational problem statement; it describes requirements but does not specify an active-active protocol.

facts.label: Uplink support goal
facts.value: Two up to at least four

today: RFC 7379 is an Informational problem statement and has not been obsoleted or updated according to the batch metadata. The Appointed Forwarder mechanism it discusses is specified in RFC 6439.

sections.title: Active-Active at the TRILL Edge
sections.content:
TRILL supports loop-free multipath forwarding inside a campus. Active-active connection extends load sharing and fast recovery to an end station with multiple links to edge RBridges.

The Appointed Forwarder mechanism allows only one RBridge to send native frames for a given VLAN on a link. In a multi-switch LAALP attachment, the customer equipment does not forward the Hello packets that let edge RBridges coordinate, so each may believe it is appointed.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside TRILL, traffic can use multiple paths. At the edge, several switches may each think they alone should forward traffic for the same VLAN.

sections.title: Customer Equipment and Edge Groups
sections.content:
The RFC calls an end station or bridge customer equipment (CE). A Local Active-Active Link Protocol (LAALP) runs across the CE, its links, and the edge RBridges; MC-LAG is one example of a similar arrangement.

An edge group is the set of edge RBridges to which at least one CE is multiply attached using a LAALP. The document assumes the members can exchange information and learn promptly when a member or link fails.
sections.plainLanguage: A LAALP coordinates a device's connections to several switches. The edge group is the set of switches connected to that device through this arrangement.

sections.title: Four Problems to Solve
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four problems. Multi-destination frames can reach the CE more than once; a frame from the CE can loop back to it; remote RBridges can keep relearning one MAC address against different nicknames; and group members can lack each other's learned address mappings.

The address flip-flop can overwrite previous learning and may reorder returning traffic. Unsynchronized mappings can make a member flood unknown-unicast traffic that another member could have forwarded directly.
sections.plainLanguage: Frames can arrive more than once or return to their sender. Switches can also disagree about where a device is, or flood traffic because they lack a neighbor's information.

sections.title: Requirements for a Solution
sections.content:
A solution MUST keep all CE uplinks active, prevent loops and duplicate frames, and prevent learned address-to-nickname mappings from flip-flopping. Packets for a flow SHOULD stay in order, and the Reverse Path Forwarding Check MUST continue to work.

The solution SHOULD need little configuration, detect group misconfiguration, support gradual deployment by changing edge RBridges, and work with two up to at least four active-active uplinks. It must not require a dedicated physical link between edge RBridges.
sections.plainLanguage: A fix must let every uplink work while preventing loops, duplicates, and unstable address learning. It should also be possible to deploy at the edge without upgrading the whole campus.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This Informational overview says it adds no extra security risks. Risks from a particular LAALP or solution are left to the documents describing those mechanisms.

The RFC suggests considering link security on the Ethernet links to protect end-station data and link-level control messages, including LAALP messages. It refers readers to RFC 6325 for general TRILL security.
sections.plainLanguage: This document describes the problem, not a new protocol. It points to link security as a way to protect traffic and control messages on the edge links.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PROBLEMS AT THE TRILL EDGE

items.label: Frame duplication
items.desc: The CE may receive several copies of a multi-destination frame.

items.label: Loopback
items.desc: A frame sent by the CE can be sent back to it by another edge member.

items.label: Address flip-flop
items.desc: Remote RBridges can relearn one address against different nicknames.

items.label: Unsynchronized information
items.desc: A member may flood traffic because it lacks another member's mapping.
